reception.text: The newspapers filled with 'conservation,' and a word that had been Forest Service jargon became a household term almost overnight.
The governors adopted their declaration by voice vote 'without dissenting voice.'
reception.source: Proceedings of a Conference of Governors (1909), p. 201

reception.text: Governor Joseph W. Folk of Missouri objected that the declaration would give the presidency a standing power to summon the governors.
reception.source: Proceedings of a Conference of Governors (1909)

reception.text: By January 1909, 36 states and territories had formed conservation commissions of their own, up from 33 in December 1908.
reception.source: Pinchot to Roosevelt, Jan. 11, 1909, Report of the National Conservation Commission, p. 12

political_impact.text: Roosevelt appointed the 48-member National Conservation Commission by letter, with Gifford Pinchot as chairman.
political_impact.source: Report of the National Conservation Commission, S. Doc. 676

political_impact.text: Roosevelt sent Congress the Commission's report, 'the first inventory of its natural resources ever made by any nation.'
The House voted 140 to 60 on a division to make in order Tawney's ban on funding or staffing commissions not authorized by law.
political_impact.source: Congressional Record, 60th Cong., 2d sess., vol. 43, p. 3120

political_impact.text: Section 9 of the Sundry Civil Appropriations Act barred paying for or detailing staff to unauthorized commissions, cutting off the National Conservation Commission.
A North American Conservation Conference of the United States, Canada, Newfoundland and Mexico met at the White House and adopted a declaration of principles.
The State Department circulated an invitation to a world conservation congress at The Hague, signed by Acting Secretary Alvey A. Adee.
political_impact.source: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1909, Doc. 1

political_impact.text: Secretary Knox recast the Hague invitation as a preliminary inquiry after Dutch protests, and the congress never met.
political_impact.source: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1909, Doc. 2

political_impact.text: The Ballinger–Pinchot quarrel split the conservation movement; Taft directed Pinchot's removal as Forester on January 7, 1910, and Ballinger resigned in March 1911.
political_impact.source: Taft to Pinchot, Jan. 7, 1910; Associated Press, Mar. 14, 1911

legacy.text: The National Governors Association dates its founding to the 1908 conference; the governors adopted articles of organization at Richmond in 1912.
The governors' body took the name National Governors' Conference in 1965 and National Governors Association in 1977.
legacy.source: Proceedings of the National Governors' Conference, 1965, p. 13; research entry

legacy.text: The 1909 ban on funding unauthorized commissions survives in the United States Code.

today.name: National Governors Association
today.note: Dates its founding to the 1908 conference, though it became a standing body only in 1912.
